title: Glasshouse and Radiators
premise: Marguerite Blackwood, a bridge inspector who measures everything—including her marriage to composer Elias—in tolerances and expansion joints, has spent thirty years cataloguing what they never said to each other. When a song drifts through her car radio, a song Elias wrote for her decades ago and never recorded, she realizes the music is a doorway: he is dying, and the song is pulling them both into the unfinished rooms of their shared memory. Inside, they must confront the silence around their stillborn daughter, the betrayal Marguerite committed, and the justice Elias sought outside the courts. The story ends with Elias's death at dawn, Marguerite finally speaking her inventory aloud at his graveside, and her choosing to record the song at last—her voice, his melody, the goodbye complete.
about_author: Wren Yarrow is a former structural drafter who spent a decade inspecting bridges across the northern counties before turning to fiction, and the precision of that work still shows in every sentence. Their stories examine how people build lives the way they build spans—assuming the load will hold—and have appeared in several small literary journals.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Marguerite, in her POV, inspects the Harrow Bridge, measuring gaps that widen in heat and narrow in cold, and privately compares them to the silences in her marriage. She returns home to Elias, who no longer plays piano, and catalogs three things she doesn't say over dinner. Emotional beat: the quiet dread of a life measured too carefully.

chapters.title: The Song That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Driving home through fog, Marguerite hears a melody on the radio—'Lantern for the Stairwell'—a piece Elias wrote for her in their first year and destroyed before anyone heard it. The DJ announces no such track exists. She sits in the driveway until the signal dies. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: vertigo, the past asserting itself.

chapters.title: Elias at the Window
chapters.summary: Elias's POV: he has been hearing the song for weeks, growing clearer each night, and has begun writing down what he remembers of it. He watches Marguerite's car in the driveway and understands, with a calm that frightens him, that he is being summoned somewhere. Emotional beat: acceptance arriving before fear.

chapters.title: Inventory of the Unsaid
chapters.summary: Marguerite reveals her private notebook—decades of entries cataloguing every withheld sentence, starting with the night they lost their daughter, June. Elias finds it while looking for batteries. Neither speaks of it; he simply sets it back exactly as it was. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: exposure without confrontation.

chapters.title: The Doorway Opens
chapters.summary: Playing the recovered melody together at the piano, the couple is pulled inside the music itself: they stand in the kitchen of their first apartment, 1989, young versions of themselves moving around them like ghosts. They cannot change anything here—only witness. POV: alternating. Emotional beat: wonder shadowed by helplessness.

chapters.title: Rules of the House
chapters.summary: Inside the song, they learn its logic: each room is a memory neither of them ever spoke aloud, and the song will only release them when every room has been entered and named. The radio in the real world is their tether. Elias's cough—real, medical—bleeds through. POV: Elias. Emotional beat: the stakes sharpen; time is finite.

chapters.title: June's Room
chapters.summary: The nursery they never furnished. Marguerite finally says the name June aloud for the first time in thirty years while Elias admits he blamed her silently, wrongly, and carried the accusation like a stone. They grieve together inside the memory. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: catharsis, the first true unburdening.

chapters.title: What Marguerite Did
chapters.summary: A room Marguerite has dreaded: 1994, the year she sold Elias's unfinished symphony to a rival composer to pay their debts, letting him believe he'd simply lost the manuscript. Inside, Elias watches her do it and says nothing—yet. POV: Elias. Emotional beat: betrayal surfacing, the marriage's fault line exposed.

chapters.title: The Rival's House
chapters.summary: Back in the present, Marguerite tracks down Theo Vance, the composer who profited, and finds him old, celebrated, and hollow—his greatest work not even his. She demands nothing; she only tells him she knows. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: justice as witness, not punishment.

chapters.title: Elias's Verdict
chapters.summary: Inside the song, Elias constructs a room of his own: the night he decided, years ago, to stop playing rather than confront her. He realizes he chose silence as his own quiet punishment, and that his silence punished them both. POV: Elias. Emotional beat: complicity recognized; anger softening into sorrow.

chapters.title: Diagnosis
chapters.summary: The real world intrudes: Elias's cough is pancreatic cancer, months at most. In the hospital corridor Marguerite reads her inventory notebook and understands she has been rehearsing this goodbye her whole life without knowing it. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: terror transmuted into resolve.

chapters.title: The Rooms Multiply
chapters.summary: Inside the song, unspoken memories begin appearing faster and darker—the affair Marguerite almost had, the letter Elias wrote and burned, his mother's funeral he skipped. The song is accelerating, and the tether to the radio weakens each visit. POV: alternating. Emotional beat: urgency; the house of memory is collapsing inward.

chapters.title: Theo's Confession
chapters.summary: Theo Vance, confronted by his own hollow rooms, publicly credits Elias with the symphony in an interview Marguerite arranges. Justice outside the law: not a courtroom, but the record corrected. Elias, watching from his hospital bed, weeps. POV: Elias. Emotional beat: restitution, bittersweet and late.

chapters.title: The Burned Letter
chapters.summary: The song reconstructs the letter Elias burned in 2001—a confession that he'd known about the stolen symphony all along and stayed anyway. Marguerite reads it in his handwriting inside the memory and finally understands the marriage's strange, stubborn devotion. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: devastating tenderness.

chapters.title: Almost
chapters.summary: Marguerite's almost-affair with a young engineer, 2003. Inside the memory she stops herself this time, walks the hallway she never walked, and tells Elias why she turned back: not duty, but the unfinished song between them. POV: alternating. Emotional beat: forgiveness asked and given in the same breath.

chapters.title: The Last Unspoken
chapters.summary: One room remains, but neither can find it. Elias weakens; the radio signal frays. Marguerite rereads her inventory and realizes the final unsaid thing is her own: 'I love you,' never once spoken in thirty years because her mother taught her love was a debt, not a gift. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: the barrier is hers alone now.

chapters.title: The Room That Is Marguerite
chapters.summary: The last room is her childhood kitchen, her mother's silence, the origin of the inventory. Marguerite enters it alone—Elias cannot follow—and speaks to the ghost of her mother, breaking the inheritance of silence. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: the climax of the inner journey; the chain broken.

chapters.title: I Love You
chapters.summary: At his hospital bedside, radio playing the song faintly, Marguerite says the three words aloud, then reads him her entire inventory, entry by entry, every unsaid thing finally said. Elias answers with his own list. The song's rooms empty around them. POV: alternating. Emotional beat: the emotional climax; thirty years released.

chapters.title: Dawn Session
chapters.summary: In the song's final room—the empty concert hall from their first date—Elias plays 'Lantern for the Stairwell' one last time while Marguerite, in the real world, holds a recorder to the radio, capturing it at last. The music begins to fade as the song completes itself. POV: Elias. Emotional beat: triumph and imminent loss intertwined.

chapters.title: Goodbye, Properly
chapters.summary: Elias dies at dawn with Marguerite's hand on his chest, the recorded song playing softly. Inside the music's last fading room, they say goodbye out loud, face to face, before the doorway closes forever. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: grief fully inhabited, not deferred.

chapters.title: The Graveside Reading
chapters.summary: Marguerite speaks at the funeral—not a eulogy but her inventory's final entry, read aloud, telling the mourners everything, including June's name and the stolen symphony. Theo Vance stands at the back and does not look away. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: public truth as the final act of justice.

chapters.title: Lantern for the Stairwell
chapters.summary: A year later, Marguerite releases the recording—her voice over Elias's melody—and inspects the Harrow Bridge one last time before retiring, leaving her notebook in the bridge's maintenance archive for whoever comes after. She hums the song as she walks away, out loud, into the ordinary day. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: quiet, earned peace.
